narrative:
The model predicted a 67.4% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your first year and again at the end of your third year were the two strongest influences, both pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. In both cases you placed in the second decile, far below the average of roughly sixth decile among students who were accepted. These consistently low rankings signaled to the model that you might struggle with the demands of law school and the bar exam.

Your undergraduate GPA of 3.70 worked in the opposite direction. It is noticeably higher than the 3.23 average of accepted students and therefore pulled the prediction toward passing. However, this positive signal was not large enough to overcome the negative impact of your class rankings.

The model also noted your LSAT score of 31, which sits below the 37.18 average of accepted applicants, but this was less influential than your school performance.

You should focus on strengthening the areas the model weighed most heavily. Retaking the LSAT to raise your score, or spending time improving your study habits and academic performance before reapplying, would directly address the factors that led to this rejection. Many students improve these metrics on a second attempt and are admitted.
